query: Eutectic high-entropy alloys contain dual-phase lamellar colonies with numerous internal boundaries, where microcracking can initiate and lead to catastrophic damage during room-temperature tensile deformation. Conventional processing commonly raises strength at the expense of ductility, while the wide range of previously proposed microstructural-design and processing strategies has not eliminated room-temperature brittleness and limited tensile ductility. Under these constraints, what single intervention could improve both strength and room-temperature tensile ductility? State one testable hypothesis that identifies the intervention, explains its mechanism, predicts outcomes relative to the unmodified lamellar-colony baseline, defines its boundary conditions, cites supporting prior evidence, and proposes an experiment whose result would falsify the hypothesis.

generation.hypothesis: Tailoring the phase-boundary morphology to be serrated rather than planar via a single, controlled thermo‐mechanical processing step will improve both room‐temperature tensile strength and ductility in eutectic high-entropy alloys. This improvement is achieved by creating serrated interfaces that distribute localized stresses and delay microcrack nucleation.
generation.material_initial_state: A eutectic HEA (e.g. AlCoCrFeNi2.1) in the as-cast condition with dual-phase lamellar colonies having predominantly straight (planar) phase boundaries that are prone to microcrack nucleation during tensile deformation.
generation.intervention: Apply a single, carefully calibrated thermo‐mechanical treatment (for example, a high strain-rate rolling at an intermediate temperature) designed to perturb the lamellar morphology and induce serrated (non-planar) phase boundaries.
generation.conditions: Room-temperature tensile loading; processing parameters (strain rate, temperature, and deformation degree) optimized to avoid phase coarsening while specifically inducing interface serration without altering the overall phase fractions.
generation.structural_mediator: Serrated phase boundaries that increase boundary curvature and local heterogeneity in the lamellar colonies.
generation.mechanism: Serrated phase boundaries are expected to act as more effective barriers to microcrack nucleation and propagation by distributing localized stress concentrations and promoting strain hardening, thereby overcoming the conventional trade-off between strength and ductility.
generation.predicted_outcome: Compared to the as-cast baseline, the processed HEA will show a higher yield strength along with an increased uniform tensile elongation, along with evidence (via microscopy) of reduced microcrack initiation at the now serrated interfaces.
generation.baseline: Eutectic HEA with cast, straight lamellar colonies that provide high strength but limited ductility due to facile microcrack initiation and propagation along planar phase boundaries.
generation.boundary: The approach is effective only if the intrinsic microstructural stability allows the transition from planar to serrated interfaces without deleterious phase coarsening or loss of the dual-phase architecture; overprocessing or inappropriate temperature/strain conditions may negate benefits.
generation.uncertainty: Exact processing parameters needed to optimize serration, and the magnitude of simultaneous improvements in strength and ductility remain to be fully quantified.

falsification_experiment.design: Prepare two sets of samples of the target eutectic HEA. One set is kept in the as-cast condition (baseline) and the other is processed via the proposed thermo‐mechanical treatment intended to induce serrated phase boundaries. Use SEM/TEM and EBSD to confirm the change in phase-boundary morphology. Conduct standardized room-temperature tensile tests on both sets.
measurements: Fractographic analysis for microcrack initiation (location, density) via microscopy
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If the processed samples do not show statistically significant increases in both yield strength and tensile ductility compared to the baseline, or if microcrack initiation along the serrated boundaries is not reduced (as evidenced by similar or worsened fracture behavior), then the hypothesis is falsified.
